title: De altitudine columnarum sub proprio pondere corruentium

deep.reconstruction:
Problem: how tall can a uniform vertical column be before it bends under its own weight (Euler's self-weight buckling problem)? Take the vertical abscissa AX = x, measured down from the free top A, and the horizontal deflection XY = y. Euler recalls his earlier equilibrium equation ∫x dy + E d²y/dx² = 0. Here E is the bending stiffness divided by the weight per unit length. The term ∫x dy is the moment at X of the weight of the column above X, taken as proportional to arc length, which is approximately x.

Differentiating once and writing p = dy/dx gives E p'' + x p = 0. This is the Airy equation in the scaled variable t = x/E^{1/3}. The page's conditions are: zero moment at the free top, so y''(0) = 0 and p'(0) = 0; y(0) = 0; and p(0) = A.

The resulting power series is y/A = x − x^4/(2·3·4 E) + 1·4 x^7/(7! E²) − 1·4·7 x^10/(10! E³) + … . I checked the first three terms against p'' = −x p/E and they are right.

In modern form p ∝ √t J_{−1/3}((2/3) t^{3/2}). With z = (2/3) t^{3/2} one has dz = √t dt, so y = A E^{1/3} c ∫_0^z J_{−1/3}(s) ds for a constant c. Each zero of p, i.e. each zero of J_{−1/3}, gives a maximum or minimum of y. These are Euler's 'innumerable maxima and minima'.

These extrema are exactly the critical lengths for a column clamped at its base and free at the top, where the base condition is y'(L) = 0. The first one, j_{−1/3,1} ≈ 1.866, gives L³ ≈ 7.84 E. That is Greenhill's 1881 result, so Euler's curve already contains it implicitly.

Euler says he was misled into thinking columns could be made indefinitely tall. Over the following pages he explains that his solution leaves the top A free, whereas a column whose top is held on the vertical line AB is a different problem.
errors: Euler says the curve meets the axis only when continued to infinity. That is wrong. As x → ∞, y tends to a nonzero limit, y∞ = A E^{1/3} ∫_0^∞ p(t)dt = A E^{1/3}/(3 Ai(0)) = A E^{1/3} 3^{−1/3} Γ(2/3) ≈ 0.939 A E^{1/3}. In Bessel form this follows from ∫_0^∞ J_ν = 1 for ν > −1. The curve therefore approaches a vertical line parallel to the axis, not the axis itself.

His observation that all the ordinates lie on one side of the axis is correct (y > 0 for x > 0). However, it is a nontrivial fact: it is equivalent to the positivity of ∫_0^z J_{−1/3}(s) ds. As I recall this was proved in the 20th century (Cooke; Makai) for −1 < ν, but I am not certain of the attribution. Euler gives no proof.
Modelling simplification: the weight above X is taken proportional to x rather than to arc length. This is acceptable to first order.
Truesdell's assessment is that Euler's 1778 self-weight papers failed to reach the correct buckling criterion, and that the correct one was found by Greenhill in 1881.

ideas.what: Differential equation of a column bending under its own weight, ∫x dy + E y'' = 0, equivalent to an Airy equation for the slope
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (1778 papers); correct solution by Greenhill 1881
ideas.where_published: Euler's companion column papers in Acta Acad. Petrop. 1778 (E508–E510); discussed in Truesdell, Rational Mechanics of Flexible or Elastic Bodies (Opera omnia II.11/2)

ideas.what: Power-series solution with coefficients 1·4·7…/(3n+1)!, i.e. an Airy-type series
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (series); Airy 1838 (function); Bessel functions in general

ideas.what: The curve's ordinates have infinitely many maxima and minima, all on one side of the axis
ideas.modern_name: Positivity of ∫_0^x J_ν(t)dt for ν = −1/3; the extrema at zeros of J_{−1/3} give clamped–free critical heights
ideas.usually_credited_to: Positivity: Cooke / Makai (20th c.), attribution uncertain; critical height L³ = 7.837 EI/q: Greenhill 1881

missed.claim: Euler's empirical remark that all ordinates of the 'wonderful curve' lie on one side of the axis is the statement ∫_0^z J_{−1/3}(s)ds > 0. That is an instance of a 20th-century positivity theorem for Bessel integrals, related to the Askey–Steinig circle of problems. His maxima and minima occur at zeros of J_{−1/3}, which give Greenhill's clamped–free critical heights.
missed.quote: innumerabiles applicatas, tam maximas quam minimas, continens, quae autem omnes ad eandem partem axis verticalis sitae videbantur
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is a historical curiosity: an 18th-century numerical observation of a Bessel-integral positivity property. Specialists in elastic stability history (Truesdell) already know the problem well, so it is of minor interest.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a well-known episode, Euler's flawed self-weight column analysis, which Truesdell examined in detail. The only small extras are the link to positivity of ∫J_{−1/3} and the fact that the 'asymptote to the axis' claim is actually wrong. Neither is significant.
transcription_corrections: The transcription is essentially correct. The denominators read '2.3.4.E', '2.…7 E²' and '2.…10 E³', with numerators 1·x^4, 1·4·x^7 and 1·4·7·x^10, matching the image.
